timelineEvents.title: Arrival in New York en route to Los Angeles
timelineEvents.label: 24 Oct 1934 · Arrival in New York
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper arrived in New York from France with Eleonora on a temporary visa, travelling onward to Los Angeles.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Kaper and his wife Eleonora sailed from Le Havre on 17 October 1934 aboard the S.S. Champlain in second cabin class and reached New York on 24 October. Their non-immigrant visas had been issued in Paris on 15 October, numbered in a single series with the Jurmanns’ (NI 1581–1584), and the manifest records Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer as having paid the passage and as the party they were joining in Culver City. Kaper gave his occupation as musician and declared that he meant to stay about eight months and then return, without seeking United States citizenship. David Blum of the Culver Export Corporation met them in New York, and they left for Hollywood on 27 October.

timelineEvents.title: Entry for permanent residence
timelineEvents.label: 1 Nov 1935 · Permanent U.S. entry
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper entered the United States for permanent residence through Calexico with Eleonora.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Kaper entered for permanent residence at Calexico, California, from Mexicali on 1 November 1935, travelling on foot with Eleonora. The manifest records 6626 Franklin Ave., Hollywood, as his U.S. destination; his Declaration of Intention four months later records the same address as his residence. The crossing followed the Immigration and Naturalization Service pre-examination procedure: Kaper gave the Commercial Hotel in Mexicali as his last permanent residence abroad and entered on a consular immigration visa, C.I.V. no. 1/24, issued there under Section 5 of the Immigration Act of 1924 and charged to the Polish quota. The manifest records his previous stay in California from 24 October 1934 to 20 October 1935, and his Polish passport no. 10568, issued by the Consulate General in Paris on 5 August 1934 and expired on 25 August 1935.

timelineEvents.title: Hollywood debut
timelineEvents.label: 1935 · Hollywood debut
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper made his Hollywood debut at MGM, contributing songs to Escapade and other studio films.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Kaper contributed to Escapade, directed by Robert Z. Leonard and starring William Powell and Luise Rainer. For the film, which opened in July 1935, he supplied a single number, “You’re All I Need”, to words by Gus Kahn. He also contributed songs to the Marx Brothers’ A Night at the Opera, with Ned Washington, and to Mutiny on the Bounty. MGM engaged him at first as a song specialist rather than as a composer of film scores; by his own account, he moved between those roles only gradually. The press introduced Kaper and Jurmann as “Two New Composers” of Kiepura’s European hits.

timelineEvents.title: San Francisco success and Three Smart Girls
timelineEvents.label: 1936 · San Francisco and Three Smart Girls
timelineEvents.shortDescription: The title song from San Francisco became a major hit, while Kaper and Jurmann also contributed to Universal’s Three Smart Girls.
timelineEvents.longDescription: The success of San Francisco made Kaper and Jurmann more visible in Hollywood and helped establish Kaper’s reputation beyond the MGM studio system. They also contributed to Three Smart Girls, the Universal production associated with Deanna Durbin and Joseph Pasternak. Tommy Dorsey’s recording of the San Francisco title song stood third in the Victor column of The Billboard’s ten best records for the week ended 3 August 1936.

timelineEvents.title: Declarations of Intention
timelineEvents.label: 4 Feb 1936 · Declarations of Intention
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Bronisław and Eleonora Kaper filed Declarations of Intention to become U.S. citizens in Los Angeles.
timelineEvents.longDescription: On 4 February 1936, Bronisław Kaper and Eleonora Kaper each filed a Declaration of Intention in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California, Los Angeles. Bronisław Kaper’s declaration records him as residing at Château des Fleurs, 6626 Franklin Ave., Hollywood. A Certificate of Arrival issued on 2 January 1936 had confirmed the Calexico entry, in a document valid, as its own form states, for naturalisation purposes only; its number, 23-46078, recurs on the declaration and ties the two documents together.

timelineEvents.title: European Film Fund established
timelineEvents.label: 1938 · European Film Fund
timelineEvents.shortDescription: The European Film Fund was established in 1938 to aid refugees from the European film community; a later donor list documents Kaper’s involvement.
timelineEvents.longDescription: The European Film Fund was established in 1938 by Paul Kohner, Ernst Lubitsch and Carl Laemmle to aid refugees arriving from Europe. Kaper’s involvement is documented by a surviving donor list covering 1 May 1941–30 April 1942, which records “Kaper, Bronislaw” and a contribution of $120. The list does not establish when he first became involved.

timelineEvents.title: End of the Jurmann–Kaper partnership
timelineEvents.label: 1938 · Jurmann–Kaper era ends
timelineEvents.shortDescription: The Jurmann–Kaper collaboration ended amicably as Hollywood’s musical priorities changed.
timelineEvents.longDescription: The Jurmann–Kaper collaboration ended amicably as changes in the film industry reduced demand for thematic songs.

timelineEvents.title: Kaper’s solo career at MGM
timelineEvents.label: 1939 · Solo MGM chapter begins
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper remained at MGM and continued his career independently after the partnership with Jurmann ended.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Kaper stayed at MGM after the partnership with Jurmann ended and moved, by his own account gradually, from writing songs to composing film scores.

timelineEvents.title: MGM markets Kaper and Jurmann as “Viennese composers”
timelineEvents.label: MGM’s “Viennese” label
timelineEvents.shortDescription: American studio publicity recast Kaper and Jurmann as a Viennese composing team, turning “Vienna” into a promotional brand rather than a biographical fact.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Soon after their arrival at MGM, the American press and studio publicity presented Kaper and Jurmann as “Viennese composers”. The label suited MGM’s first use of the duo in Escapade, a Hollywood remake of the Viennese film Maskerade, but it was biographically misleading for Kaper, whose career had developed in Warsaw and Berlin. The event marks the moment when Hollywood began to translate his European professional history into a marketable studio identity. The label outlasted their arrival: in December 1936 the Viennese paper Telegraf itself wrote of “die Wiener Komponisten Kaper und Jurmann”.

places.publicNote: Los Angeles provides the metropolitan context for Kaper’s Hollywood career after his move to MGM.
